newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist win would not derail EMU - analysts.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist win would not derail EMU - analysts.

text.p: The French election appears to be turning into a close contest between the ruling centre-right and the left-wing opposition but a Socialist win would be unlikely to derail European monetary union, economists said on Friday.
"They may want a softer EMU (economic and monetary union) but it's quite unlikely they (the Socialists) have any idea of abandoning it," said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard.
But French and other European markets could face turmoil until it became clear what policies the new administration would adopt.

The leadup to the two-round elections on May 25 and June 1 promises to be volatile with shorter-dated French government debt taking most of the impact, economists said. "It's going to be a bouncy ride between now and then," said Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais.
An opinion poll on Thursday seemed to throw the race wide open, predicting only a wafer-thin parliamentary majority for the centre-right.
The IPSOS poll suggested the ruling coalition would win 292 seats in the 577-member National Assembly with the Socialists capturing 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front one.

Another poll published on Friday showed a majority of French voters believed conservative President Jacques Chirac had failed to honour most of his campaign promises, including his hallmark pledge to roll back unemployment, now at a record 12.8 percent.
Market reaction to the polls on Friday was relatively muted with bond and stock prices slightly lower.

During past EMU jitters, investors switched into German assets, analysts said. But now some are said to be moving into Swiss assets, suggesting they expect the euro to be launched but as a weaker currency.

The markets are relatively optimistic that the centre-right will win. But some economists say Chirac's decision to call the snap vote to clear the decks for further austerity and ensure France qualifies for the single currency could backfire.

Several economists also say the vote could become a referendum on monetary union. Many voters have made EMU a scapegoat for France's economic troubles because of the austerity required to achieve it. The single currency was approved by the thinnest of margins in a 1992 referendum.

But if the Socialists came to power "they cannot pretend it (the Maastricht treaty) was something they inherited from the conservatives," said Steven Englander of Smith Barney in Paris. "I don't think when push comes to shove they can walk away."

It was the Socialists under the late French president Francois Mitterrand who signed the Maastricht treaty. "A large majority of the socialist electorate is in favour of EMU and (Socialist leader) Lionel Jospin himself has always been so," Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley said.

Jospin's platform opposes further fiscal restraint to meet the Maastricht criteria and stresses the need to include Italy in the first wave of entrants. His other proposals include a shorter working week without pay cuts and a plan to shift the tax burden from employee income to capital income.

If he becomes prime minister, Jospin "would probably pursue EMU plans", said Jean-Francois Mercier of Salomon Brothers. "He has repeatedly rejected pressure from the party's left wing to endorse an EMU delay," he said.
However, Mercier said the need to maintain the electoral alliance with the Communist Party would mean that a pro-EMU strategy would not take shape until after the election.
Philippe Ithurbide of Societe Generale said there was no doubt, however, that if the Socialists came to power, the "unity of the Franco-German 'couple' would be a little bit weaker".
The market upside to a decisive conservative win could be considerable.

"If the coalition gets back in with (a majority of) 50 seats, that puts them in an incredibly powerful position," said Lindsay. "They would have five years to implement their plans. They could transform France in that time."

The centre-right would also be in the lucky situation of embarking on the talks leading to monetary union unchallenged domestically and be able to implement the tough public spending measures necessary to keep down France's budget deficit.
